title: Linear independence & linear transformations
summary: When a set of vectors has no redundancy, and how every linear map ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is a matrix whose columns are the images of the standard basis. One-to-one and onto reduce to pivots in every column and every row.

blocks.text: {v₁, …, vₚ} is linearly independent if c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ = 0 forces c₁ = ⋯ = cₚ = 0. Otherwise it is dependent, and a nontrivial solution is a dependence relation.

blocks.name: Columns test
blocks.text: The columns of A are linearly independent ⇔ Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution ⇔ no free variables ⇔ a pivot in every column.

proof.text: c₁a₁ + ⋯ + cₙaₙ = 0 is literally Ac = 0. A free variable would let us choose a nonzero c.

blocks.text: Independence means no vector is redundant: removing any one shrinks the span. Dependence means some vector can be built from the others.

blocks.name: Characterization of dependent sets
blocks.text: A set of two or more vectors is dependent ⇔ at least one vector is a linear combination of the others. In fact, if v₁ ≠ 0, some vⱼ (j > 1) is a combination of the preceding vectors v₁, …, vⱼ₋₁.

proof.text: Take a dependence relation and let j be the largest index with cⱼ ≠ 0. Solve for vⱼ: vⱼ = −(c₁/cⱼ)v₁ − ⋯ − (cⱼ₋₁/cⱼ)vⱼ₋₁.

blocks.title: Test independence and find a relation
blocks.prompt: Are v₁ = (1, 2, 3), v₂ = (4, 5, 6), v₃ = (2, 1, 0) independent? If not, find a dependence relation.
steps: Row reduce [v₁ v₂ v₃]: R₂ − 2R₁ → [0 −3 −3], R₃ − 3R₁ → [0 −6 −6], R₃ − 2R₂ → [0 0 0].
Only 2 pivots for 3 columns ⇒ x₃ is free ⇒ dependent.

blocks.name: More vectors than entries ⇒ dependent
blocks.text: If p > n, any set {v₁, …, vₚ} in ℝⁿ is linearly dependent.

proof.text: The n×p matrix [v₁ ⋯ vₚ] has at most n pivots (one per row), so at least p − n ≥ 1 columns have no pivot. That column gives a free variable, hence a nontrivial solution of Ac = 0, which is a dependence relation.

blocks.title: Dependence relations among four vectors in ℝ⁴ (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: v₁ = (1, 2, 0, 1), v₂ = (0, 1, 1, 1), v₃ = (2, 3, −1, 1), v₄ = (1, 0, −2, −1). Find all dependence relations and a basis of their span.
steps: Row reduce [v₁ v₂ v₃ v₄] to RREF [1 0 2 1; 0 1 −1 −2; 0 0 0 0; 0 0 0 0]: pivots in columns 1, 2; x₃, x₄ free.
x₁ = −2x₃ − x₄, x₂ = x₃ + 2x₄. Null space basis (−2, 1, 1, 0) and (−1, 2, 0, 1).
Relations: −2v₁ + v₂ + v₃ = 0 (so v₃ = 2v₁ − v₂) and −v₁ + 2v₂ + v₄ = 0 (so v₄ = v₁ − 2v₂). Every relation is a combination of these two.
The RREF columns 3 and 4 literally contain these weights: column 3 is (2, −1) and column 4 is (1, −2).
blocks.answer: v₃ = 2v₁ − v₂, v₄ = v₁ − 2v₂; {v₁, v₂} is a basis of the span (a plane in ℝ⁴).

lesson.title: Independence by inspection, and parameter questions

items: One vector: independent iff it is nonzero.
Two vectors: dependent iff one is a multiple of the other.
Contains 0: always dependent (1·0 = 0 is a nontrivial relation).
More vectors than entries (p > n in ℝⁿ): always dependent, since the n×p matrix has at most n pivots, fewer than p columns.
A subset of an independent set is independent; a superset of a dependent set is dependent.

blocks.text: For three or more vectors, 'no vector is a multiple of another' does NOT give independence: (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0) are pairwise non-parallel but dependent.
Why 4 vectors in ℝ³ are always dependent: [v₁ v₂ v₃ v₄] is 3×4, so at most 3 pivots and at least one free variable, i.e. a nontrivial solution of Ac = 0.

blocks.title: Parameter for dependence
blocks.prompt: For which h are (1, −1, 4), (3, −5, 7), (−1, 5, h) dependent? Give the relation.
steps: Three vectors in ℝ³: dependent ⇔ det [v₁ v₂ v₃] = 0 (or: row reduction loses a pivot).
A pivot is lost exactly when h = 6.
At h = 6 solve: x₃ = 1, −2x₂ + 4 = 0 ⇒ x₂ = 2, x₁ + 6 − 1 = 0 ⇒ x₁ = −5.

blocks.title: Parameter with two bad values (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: For which h are v₁ = (1, 1, 1), v₂ = (1, h, 2), v₃ = (1, h², 4) dependent? Give the relation in each case.
steps: det [v₁ v₂ v₃] = det [1 1 1; 1 h h²; 1 2 4] (det of the transpose is the same) = 1(4h − 2h²) − 1(4 − h²) + 1(2 − h) = −h² + 3h − 2 = −(h − 1)(h − 2).
Dependent ⇔ h = 1 or h = 2.
h = 1: solve av₁ + bv₂ = v₃ with v₂ = (1, 1, 2), v₃ = (1, 1, 4): a + b = 1, a + 2b = 4 ⇒ b = 3, a = −2.
blocks.answer: h = 1 or h = 2; in both cases v₃ = −2v₁ + 3v₂.

blocks.text: Factor the determinant completely. Finding only the obvious root (here h = 1) is the classic way to lose half the credit.
T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ assigns to each x in ℝⁿ (domain) a vector T(x) in ℝᵐ (codomain). The range is the set of all outputs.
T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u) for all u, v, c. Consequences: T(0) = 0 and T(cu + dv) = cT(u) + dT(v).
Every matrix transformation x ↦ Ax is linear, because A(u + v) = Au + Av and A(cu) = cAu.
A quick non-linearity test: if T(0) ≠ 0, T is not linear. T(x) = Ax + b with b ≠ 0 fails. But T(0) = 0 alone does not prove linearity (e.g. T(x, y) = (x², y)).

blocks.name: Standard matrix
blocks.text: Every linear T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ is T(x) = Ax for the unique matrix A = [T(e₁) ⋯ T(eₙ)].

proof.text: x = x₁e₁ + ⋯ + xₙeₙ, so by linearity T(x) = x₁T(e₁) + ⋯ + xₙT(eₙ), which is Ax with those columns.

blocks.text: A linear map is completely determined by where it sends a basis. To find the standard matrix: find T(eⱼ) and make them the columns. If you are given T on other vectors, use linearity to solve for T(eⱼ) first.

blocks.name: Superposition
blocks.text: If T is linear, T(c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ) = c₁T(v₁) + ⋯ + cₚT(vₚ).

proof.text: Induction on p using T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) and T(cu) = cT(u).

blocks.text: Consequences of linearity used constantly: T(0) = T(0·0) = 0·T(0) = 0; T(−u) = −T(u); and a linear map is determined by its values on any basis. In particular the images of e₁, …, eₙ determine T completely.

blocks.title: Linear or not? Standard matrix from a formula
blocks.prompt: (a) Find the standard matrix of T(x₁, x₂, x₃) = (x₁ − 4x₂ + 2x₃, 3x₂ − x₃). (b) Is S(x₁, x₂) = (x₁ + 1, 2x₂) linear? (c) Is U(x₁, x₂) = (x₁x₂, x₁) linear?
steps: (a) T(e₁) = (1, 0), T(e₂) = (−4, 3), T(e₃) = (2, −1); these are the columns: [1 −4 2; 0 3 −1]. (Equivalently, read the coefficients row by row.)
(b) S(0, 0) = (1, 0) ≠ 0, so S is not linear (it is a translation composed with a stretch).
(c) U(0) = 0, but U(2(1, 1)) = U(2, 2) = (4, 2) while 2U(1, 1) = (2, 2). Scaling fails: not linear (the product x₁x₂ is quadratic).

blocks.text: For T(x) = Ax with A m×n: the domain is ℝⁿ, the codomain is ℝᵐ, and the range is Col A (all outputs), which may be smaller than the codomain.

blocks.text: Don't memorize the table: draw where e₁ and e₂ go and write those images as the columns.

blocks.title: Standard matrix of a composition
blocks.prompt: T: ℝ² → ℝ² rotates by π/2 counterclockwise, then reflects across the x-axis. Find its standard matrix and identify T.
steps: Track e₁: rotation sends it to (0, 1); reflection across the x-axis sends that to (0, −1). So T(e₁) = (0, −1).
Track e₂: rotation sends it to (−1, 0); reflection leaves it at (−1, 0). So T(e₂) = (−1, 0).
Matrix [0 −1; −1 0]. Equivalently F·R = [1 0; 0 −1][0 −1; 1 0] (the map applied first is on the right).
Comparing with the table, this is the reflection across y = −x.
blocks.answer: [0 −1; −1 0], the reflection across the line y = −x.

blocks.title: Matrix from values on other vectors
blocks.prompt: T: ℝ² → ℝ³ is linear with T(e₁ + e₂) = (1, 2, 3) and T(e₁ − e₂) = (3, 0, −1). Find the standard matrix.
steps: Columns are T(e₁), T(e₂).

blocks.text: Putting (1, 2, 3) and (3, 0, −1) in directly as the columns is wrong: the columns must be images of e₁, e₂.

blocks.title: Projection and reflection across a line (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: Find the standard matrices of the orthogonal projection P onto the line y = 2x and of the reflection R across that line.
steps: Direction of the line u = (1, 2), u·u = 5. Projection of e₁: (e₁·u/u·u)u = (1/5)(1, 2); of e₂: (2/5)(1, 2).
P = (1/5)[1 2; 2 4]. Check: P(1, 2) = (1, 2) (on the line), P(−2, 1) = 0 (perpendicular).
Reflection keeps the line component and flips the perpendicular one: R = P − (I − P) = 2P − I = [−3/5 4/5; 4/5 3/5].
Check: R(−2, 1) = (2, −1) = −(−2, 1), and det R = −9/25 − 16/25 = −1 (reflections reverse orientation).

blocks.title: Order of composition
blocks.prompt: T reflects across y = x and then applies the horizontal shear x ↦ x + 3y. Find its matrix.
steps: Matrix of the first map F = [0 1; 1 0], of the second S = [1 3; 0 1].
T(x) = S(Fx), so the matrix is SF = [1 3; 0 1][0 1; 1 0] = [3 1; 1 0].
Check e₁: F sends it to (0, 1); the shear sends (0, 1) to (3, 1). First column (3, 1). ✓

blocks.text: Every b in ℝᵐ is the image of at least one x (range = codomain). Existence question.
Every b is the image of at most one x. Uniqueness question.

blocks.name: Kernel test
blocks.text: Linear T is one-to-one ⇔ T(x) = 0 has only the trivial solution.

proof.text: If T(u) = T(v) then T(u − v) = 0, so u = v when only 0 maps to 0. Conversely, one-to-one plus T(0) = 0 means nothing else maps to 0.

blocks.name: Pivot tests for T(x) = Ax (A is m×n)
blocks.text: T is onto ⇔ columns of A span ℝᵐ ⇔ pivot in every row. T is one-to-one ⇔ columns of A are independent ⇔ pivot in every column.

blocks.title: Decide one-to-one and onto
steps: (a) A is already in echelon form with pivots in columns 1, 2, 4: a pivot in every one of the 3 rows ⇒ onto ℝ³.
(a) Column 3 has no pivot ⇒ free variable ⇒ nontrivial kernel ⇒ not one-to-one (4 columns in ℝ³ are dependent anyway).
(b) Standard matrix [3 1; 5 7; 1 3]. Its columns are not multiples of each other ⇒ independent ⇒ one-to-one.
(b) Only 2 pivots possible for 3 rows ⇒ not onto ℝ³.
blocks.answer: (a) onto, not one-to-one. (b) one-to-one, not onto.

blocks.text: Picture: one-to-one means no two inputs collide (the kernel is only 0, so no direction is crushed); onto means every point of the codomain is hit (the columns fill ℝᵐ). A projection ℝ³ → ℝ² onto the xy-plane is onto but not one-to-one; the inclusion ℝ² → ℝ³, (x, y) ↦ (x, y, 0), is one-to-one but not onto.

blocks.title: One-to-one/onto with a parameter (exam-hard)
blocks.prompt: (a) For which h is T(x) = Ax one-to-one, where A = [1 h; 2 4; 3 6]? Can it be onto? (b) For which h is T(x) = Bx with B = [1 2 1; 0 1 h; 1 3 2] onto ℝ³?
steps: (a) Rows 2 and 3 of A are (2, 4) and (3, 6) = multiples of (1, 2). If h = 2 every row is a multiple of (1, 2): rank 1, a free variable ⇒ not one-to-one. If h ≠ 2, R₂ − 2R₁ = (0, 4 − 2h) ≠ 0 gives two pivots ⇒ one-to-one.
A is 3×2: at most 2 pivots for 3 rows ⇒ never onto.
(b) B is square, so onto ⇔ one-to-one ⇔ det B ≠ 0. det B = 1(2 − 3h) − 2(0 − h) + 1(0 − 1) = 1 − h.
Onto ⇔ h ≠ 1.
blocks.answer: (a) one-to-one iff h ≠ 2, never onto (b) onto iff h ≠ 1

blocks.title: Five classic True/False
blocks.prompt: (a) If v₁, v₂, v₃ are in ℝ³ and v₃ is not a combination of v₁, v₂, the set is independent. (b) A linear T: ℝ⁵ → ℝ³ can be one-to-one. (c) If {T(u), T(v)} is independent, so is {u, v}. (d) Any set containing 0 is dependent. (e) If a set is dependent, every vector in it is a combination of the others.
steps: (a) False: v₁ = (1, 0, 0), v₂ = (2, 0, 0), v₃ = (0, 1, 0); v₁, v₂ are already dependent.
(b) False: 3×5 matrix ⇒ at most 3 pivots ⇒ a free variable ⇒ nontrivial kernel.
(c) True: a nontrivial au + bv = 0 would give aT(u) + bT(v) = 0 nontrivially. Linear maps can destroy independence but never create it.
(d) True: 1·0 = 0 with the other weights 0.
(e) False: in {(1, 0), (2, 0), (0, 1)}, (0, 1) is not a combination of the others; only SOME vector must be.

blocks.text: For any T/F on independence, try the smallest counterexamples first: vectors with zeros, parallel pairs, or the standard basis vectors.

lesson.title: Putting it together: one matrix, every question

blocks.text: Exam problems often ask several of these questions about the same matrix. One row reduction answers all of them, because every question is a question about pivots: pivot in every column ⇔ independent columns ⇔ one-to-one; pivot in every row ⇔ spanning columns ⇔ onto.

blocks.title: Full analysis of a 3×4 matrix
blocks.prompt: A = [1 −2 3 1; 2 −4 7 0; −1 2 −2 −3], T(x) = Ax. (a) Are the columns independent? Give all dependence relations. (b) Is T one-to-one? Onto ℝ³? (c) Describe the range.
steps: RREF(A) = [1 −2 0 7; 0 0 1 −2; 0 0 0 0]: pivots in columns 1 and 3; x₂, x₄ free.
(a) Dependent (4 vectors in ℝ³ always are). Null space basis (2, 1, 0, 0) and (−7, 0, 2, 1): a₂ = −2a₁ and 2a₃ + a₄ = 7a₁, i.e. a₄ = 7a₁ − 2a₃.
(b) Free variables ⇒ nontrivial kernel ⇒ not one-to-one. Only 2 pivots for 3 rows ⇒ not onto.
(c) Range = Col A = Span{a₁, a₃} = Span{(1, 2, −1), (3, 7, −2)}, a plane through 0 in ℝ³.
blocks.answer: Dependent (a₂ = −2a₁, a₄ = 7a₁ − 2a₃); neither one-to-one nor onto; range is the plane spanned by (1, 2, −1), (3, 7, −2).

blocks.text: Read dependence relations straight off the RREF: column 4 of the RREF is (7, −2, 0), which says a₄ = 7a₁ − 2a₃ (weights on the pivot columns). This works because row operations preserve every linear relation among the columns.
Do not use the columns of the RREF as a basis for the range: they are e₁, e₂ here, which need not lie in Col A at all.

cards.front: Definition of linearly independent?

back.text: c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ = 0 only for c₁ = ⋯ = cₚ = 0. Otherwise dependent; a nontrivial solution is a dependence relation.

cards.front: Columns of A are independent ⇔ ?

back.text: A x = 0 has only the trivial solution ⇔ no free variables ⇔ pivot in every column.

cards.front: Why are 4 vectors in ℝ³ always dependent?

back.text: The 3×4 matrix has at most 3 pivots, so a column lacks a pivot ⇒ free variable ⇒ nontrivial solution of A c = 0.

cards.front: When is a set of two vectors dependent?

back.text: Exactly when one is a multiple of the other.
This shortcut fails for 3 or more vectors.

cards.front: Is a set containing 0 independent?

back.text: Never: 1·0 + 0·(others) = 0 is a nontrivial relation.

cards.front: Characterization of dependent sets (Lay Thm 7)?

back.text: Dependent ⇔ some vector is a combination of the others; if v₁ ≠ 0, some vⱼ is a combination of the preceding v₁, …, vⱼ₋₁. Not every vector need be.

cards.front: Subsets and supersets of (in)dependent sets?

back.text: Subset of independent is independent. Superset of dependent is dependent. Nothing follows the other way.

cards.front: Definition of a linear transformation, and two consequences?

back.text: T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v), T(cu) = cT(u). So T(0) = 0 and T preserves linear combinations.

cards.front: Standard matrix of linear T: ℝⁿ → ℝᵐ?

back.text: A = [T(e₁) ⋯ T(eₙ)], an m×n matrix; T(x) = A x.

cards.front: Is T(x) = A x + b linear when b ≠ 0?
Rotation by θ: matrix?

back.text: [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ] (columns are the rotated e₁, e₂).

cards.front: Reflection across y = x? across y = −x?

back.text: [0 1; 1 0] (swap coordinates); [0 −1; −1 0].

cards.front: Horizontal shear by k; projection onto the x-axis?
Matrix of 'first S, then T'?

back.text: T∘S has matrix (matrix of T)(matrix of S): the map applied first is on the right.

cards.front: T(x) = A x onto ℝᵐ ⇔ ?

back.text: Columns span ℝᵐ ⇔ pivot in every row. Impossible if A has fewer columns than rows.

cards.front: T(x) = A x one-to-one ⇔ ?

back.text: T(x) = 0 only for x = 0 ⇔ columns independent ⇔ pivot in every column. Impossible if more columns than rows.

cards.front: Can a linear T: ℝ⁵ → ℝ³ be one-to-one? Can T: ℝ² → ℝ³ be onto?

back.text: Neither. 3×5 has a free variable; 3×2 has a row without a pivot.

cards.front: If T is one-to-one and {v₁, …, vₖ} independent, is {T(v₁), …, T(vₖ)} independent?

back.text: Yes: Σcᵢ T(vᵢ) = 0 ⇒ T(Σcᵢvᵢ) = 0 ⇒ Σcᵢvᵢ = 0 ⇒ all cᵢ = 0. Without one-to-one it fails (T(x, y) = (x, 0)).

cards.front: Find a dependence relation: method?

back.text: Row reduce [v₁ ⋯ vₚ] to RREF, solve A c = 0, set the free variable to 1. The solution's entries are the weights.

cards.front: Square A: how do one-to-one and onto relate?

back.text: They are equivalent (n pivots in n rows ⇔ n pivots in n columns).

hard.title: Dependence with a parameter (two roots)

prompt.text: For which h are (1, 1, h), (1, h, 1), (h, 1, 1) linearly dependent? For each such h, give an explicit dependence relation.

hard.answer: h = 1 (v₁ − v₂ = 0) or h = −2 (v₁ + v₂ + v₃ = 0)

solution.text: det
= −(h − 1)²(h + 2). (Quick route: add all rows to row 1 to factor out h + 2, then subtract.)
Dependent ⇔ det = 0 ⇔ h = 1 or h = −2.
h = 1: all three vectors equal (1, 1, 1): e.g. v₁ − v₂ = 0.
h = −2: the sum of the three is (h + 2)(1, 1, 1) = 0, so v₁ + v₂ + v₃ = 0.
What it tests: Two roots — students often find only h = 1 (the obvious one). Always factor the full determinant.

items: 1. If v₁, v₂, v₃ ∈ ℝ³ and none is a multiple of another, then {v₁, v₂, v₃} is linearly independent.
2. If {v₁, v₂, v₃} is linearly dependent, then v₃ is a linear combination of v₁ and v₂.
3. No linear transformation ℝ⁵ → ℝ³ is one-to-one.
4. If T is linear and {T(u), T(v)} is independent, then {u, v} is independent.
5. The map T(x) = Ax + b with b ≠ 0 is linear.
1. False. (1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0): pairwise non-parallel, but the third is the sum of the first two. The “no multiples” test only works for two vectors.
2. False. v₁ = (1, 0), v₂ = (2, 0), v₃ = (0, 1). Dependent (2v₁ − v₂ = 0), but v₃ is not in Span{v₁, v₂}. The theorem only says some vector is a combination of the preceding ones.
3. True. Its 3×5 matrix has at most 3 pivots, so at least 2 free variables ⇒ nontrivial kernel.
4. True. Contrapositive: if au + bv = 0 nontrivially, apply T: aT(u) + bT(v) = 0 nontrivially.
5. False. Linear maps send 0 to 0; here T(0) = b ≠ 0.

solution.text: What it tests: Independence is about the whole set. Linear maps can destroy independence (e.g. the zero map) but can never create it.

hard.title: Rotation then reflection

prompt.text: T: ℝ² → ℝ² first rotates counterclockwise by π/3, then reflects across the line y = x. Find the standard matrix of T. Then show T is itself a reflection and find its line.

hard.answer: FR = [√3/2 1/2; 1/2 −√3/2], the reflection across the line at angle π/12 (15°)

prompt.text: T: ℝ² → ℝ³ is linear with T(e₁ + e₂) = (1, 2, 3) and T(e₁ − e₂) = (3, 0, −1). Find the standard matrix. Is T one-to-one? Onto?

solution.text: Columns not parallel ⇒ independent ⇒ one-to-one. Only 2 columns in ℝ³ ⇒ at most 2 pivots for 3 rows ⇒ not onto.
What it tests: The standard matrix needs T(eⱼ), so use linearity to solve for them. Putting (1,2,3) and (3,0,−1) directly in as columns is the classic error.

hard.title: Construct T with given range and kernel

prompt.text: Construct a linear T: ℝ³ → ℝ³ whose range is the plane x + y + z = 0 and whose kernel is the line through (1, 2, 3).

solution.text: Need columns a₁, a₂, a₃ in the plane, spanning it, with a₁ + 2a₂ + 3a₃ = 0 (that’s A(1,2,3) = 0).
Choose a₂ = (1, −1, 0), a₃ = (0, 1, −1) (independent, both in the plane); force a₁ = −2a₂ − 3a₃ = (−2, −1, 3).
. Every column sums to 0 (range ⊆ plane); rank 2, so range = plane; nullity = 3 − 2 = 1 and (1,2,3) ∈ Nul, so kernel = that line. ✓
What it tests: Rank–nullity (3 = 2 + 1) is what makes the requested data consistent. Choose the independent columns first, then define the remaining column to kill the kernel vector.

hard.title: Proof: one-to-one maps preserve independence

prompt.text: Prove: if T is linear and one-to-one and {v₁, …, vₖ} is linearly independent, then {T(v₁), …, T(vₖ)} is linearly independent. Show the hypothesis “one-to-one” cannot be dropped.

hard.answer: Σcᵢ T(vᵢ) = 0 ⇒ T(Σcᵢvᵢ) = 0 ⇒ Σcᵢvᵢ = 0 ⇒ cᵢ = 0; fails for T(x, y) = (x, 0)

solution.title: Solution
items: Suppose c₁T(v₁) + ⋯ + cₖT(vₖ) = 0. By linearity T(c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ) = 0 = T(0).
One-to-one ⇒ c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ = 0 ⇒ all cᵢ = 0 by independence. ∎
Counterexample without it: T(x, y) = (x, 0) sends the independent pair e₁, e₂ to (1,0), (0,0) — dependent.

solution.text: What it tests: One-to-one means T(u) = 0 ⇒ u = 0. Don’t try to “divide by T”.

prompt.text: Define T: ℙ₂ → ℝ² by T(p) = (p(1), p(−1)). Show T is linear, find its matrix relative to {1, t, t²} and the standard basis of ℝ², its kernel, and decide whether it is onto.

solution.text: Kernel: a + b + c = 0 and a − b + c = 0 ⇒ b = 0, c = −a: kernel = Span{t² − 1} (polynomials with roots ±1).
What it tests: Evaluation maps are linear in p (not in t). Kernel elements are polynomials, not vectors (1, 0, −1) — state both.

hard.title: Column relation gives the null space

prompt.text: (a) Find a nontrivial solution of Ax = 0. (b) Is x ↦ Ax onto ℝ³? (c) Find all solutions of Ax = a₁ + a₂ + a₃.

solution.title: Solution
items: (b) rank = 2 (two independent columns, third dependent) < 3 rows ⇒ not onto.
(c) x = (1, 1, 1) is a particular solution by inspection. Nullity = 1 so Nul A = Span{(2, −1, −1)}. All solutions: x = (1, 1, 1) + s(2, −1, −1).
(Another valid particular solution: (3, 0, 0), since a₁ + a₂ + a₃ = 3a₁. It is (1,1,1) + 1·(2,−1,−1).)

solution.text: What it tests: The coefficients of a column relation are a null vector. Don’t forget to add the null space to the particular solution.

hard.title: Onto with a parameter; describe the range

prompt.text: x onto ℝ³? For the bad value, describe the range by an equation and give a vector not in it.

hard.answer: Onto iff h ≠ 2; at h = 2 range is −2b₁ + 2b₂ + b₃ = 0, e.g. (0, 0, 1) not in it

solution.text: Square matrix: onto ⇔ det ≠ 0. det = 1(2 − h) − 2(0 − 2) + h(0 − 2) = 6 − 3h. Onto ⇔ h ≠ 2.
h = 2: reduce
Range: −2b₁ + 2b₂ + b₃ = 0. (0, 0, 1) is not in it.
What it tests: For a square matrix onto ⇔ one-to-one ⇔ det ≠ 0. For the range, row-reduce with a general b; don’t just list the columns.

keyFacts: Columns independent ⇔ A x = 0 only trivial ⇔ pivot in every column.
p vectors in ℝⁿ with p > n are dependent; any set containing 0 is dependent.
Two vectors: dependent ⇔ parallel. Three or more: pairwise non-parallel is NOT enough.
Linear ⇒ T(0) = 0; standard matrix A = [T(e₁) ⋯ T(eₙ)].
Rotation by θ: [cos θ −sin θ; sin θ cos θ]. Composition 'S then T' = (T)(S).
T(x) = A x onto ⇔ pivot in every row; one-to-one ⇔ pivot in every column ⇔ kernel = {0}.
Wide matrices are never one-to-one; tall matrices are never onto; square: both or neither.

parsons.title: One-to-one ⇔ trivial kernel
parsons.goal: Prove: a linear map T is one-to-one if and only if T(x) = 0 has only the trivial solution.
lines: If T(x) = 0 = T(0) and T is one-to-one, then x = 0.
(⇐) Assume T(x) = 0 only for x = 0, and suppose T(u) = T(v).
By linearity T(u − v) = T(u) − T(v) = 0.
So u − v = 0 by the assumption, i.e. u = v.
distractors: By linearity T(u − v) = T(u) + T(v) = 0.
If T(x) = 0, then T is onto.
So u − v ≠ 0, hence u = v.

parsons.title: One-to-one maps preserve independence
parsons.goal: Prove: if T is linear and one-to-one and {v₁, …, vₖ} is independent, then {T(v₁), …, T(vₖ)} is independent.
lines: Since T is one-to-one, its kernel is {0}, so c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ = 0.
Since {v₁, …, vₖ} is independent, c₁ = ⋯ = cₖ = 0.
So the only relation among the T(vᵢ) is the trivial one: they are independent. ∎
distractors: Since T is onto, c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₖvₖ = 0.
Since the T(vᵢ) are nonzero, every cᵢ = 0.

parsons.title: More vectors than entries are dependent
parsons.goal: Prove: if p > n, then any p vectors v₁, …, vₚ in ℝⁿ are linearly dependent.
lines: Form the n×p matrix A = [v₁ ⋯ vₚ].
Each pivot of A lies in a different row, so A has at most n pivots.
Since p > n, at least one of the p columns has no pivot.
That column corresponds to a free variable of Ac = 0.
Setting the free variable to 1 gives a nonzero solution c.
Then c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ = Ac = 0 is a nontrivial relation, so the set is dependent. ∎
distractors: Each pivot lies in a different column, so A has at most p pivots.
Since p > n, every column has a pivot.
